paragraphs.heading: Two kinds of average
paragraphs.text: The AM–GM inequality compares two ways of averaging a list of non-negative real numbers: the arithmetic mean and the geometric mean. It says the arithmetic mean is always greater than or equal to the geometric mean. The two are equal exactly when every number in the list is the same, and in that case both equal that number.

paragraphs.heading: Why it holds for two numbers
paragraphs.text: For two numbers x and y, the key fact is that (x + y)² ≥ 4xy, with equality exactly when (x − y)² = 0, that is, when x = y. Take the positive square root of both sides, divide by 2, and the two-number AM–GM inequality drops out.

paragraphs.heading: Rectangles and squares
paragraphs.text: Picture a rectangle with sides x and y. Its perimeter is 2x + 2y and its area is xy. A square with sides √xy has the same area, and its perimeter is 4√xy. AM–GM says 2x + 2y ≥ 4√xy, so among all rectangles with a given area, only the square has the smallest perimeter. This simplest case is already implicit in Euclid's Elements, Book V, Proposition 25.

paragraphs.heading: Boxes in any dimension
paragraphs.text: The full inequality stretches this picture to n dimensions. Take a box in n dimensions whose edges have lengths x₁ through xₙ. Each corner meets n edges in different directions, so the average length of those edges is (x₁ + x₂ + · · · + xₙ)/n. A cube with the same volume has edge length ⁿ√(x₁ x₂ ⋯ xₙ), which is also the average edge length at each of its corners. AM–GM then says that among boxes of equal volume, only the cube has the smallest average edge length at each corner.

paragraphs.heading: Uses in proofs and money
paragraphs.text: The inequality is useful well beyond geometry. It can be used to prove the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality. In financial mathematics, it shows that the annualized return, which is a geometric mean, is less than the average annual return, which is an arithmetic mean.

paragraphs.heading: A polynomial puzzle
paragraphs.text: It also settles a puzzle about the Motzkin polynomial. This polynomial in x and y never goes below zero, and yet it cannot be written as a sum of squares of polynomials. To show it is nonnegative, apply AM–GM to the three numbers x⁴ y², x² y⁴ and 1. Simplifying and multiplying through by 3 turns the result into exactly the claim that the polynomial is at least 0.

paragraphs.heading: Many ways to prove it
paragraphs.text: The general case can be proved in several ways. One proof uses mathematical induction and nothing beyond well-known rules of arithmetic. Another, which goes back essentially to Augustin Louis Cauchy and appears in his Cours d'analyse, uses a rarely seen technique called forward-backward induction.
